overview: Bundelkhand is a central Indian region with several states and communities, rather than one continuous kingdom. Around 1800, Bundela rulers and Maratha interests faced expanding East India Company power. The atlas shows 1800 to 1815, but its outline is misplaced: it excludes Jhansi, Orchha, Banda, Panna and Khajuraho while reaching Kolkata and Dhaka. It must not be read as Bundelkhand’s historical border. This card follows the named region; earlier Chandela and Bundela achievements and later community evidence are clearly dated.

periods.title: Atlas window: an unreliable outline
periods.summary: These imported endpoints mark map coverage, not the founding or disappearance of Bundelkhand.

items.text: The Chandelas of medieval Khajuraho and the later Bundelas of Orchha were different ruling lineages. Orchha became a Bundela capital in the sixteenth century and remained a capital until 1783. Its palaces already had long histories when this atlas window begins; the region was not newly founded in 1800.

Chhatrasal’s rebellion against Mughal authority began in 1671. His alliance with the Marathas helped reshape Bundelkhand’s politics, and Maratha interests expanded during the eighteenth century. Royal families and local chiefs retained different positions within this changing landscape. A regional name cannot tell us that every town obeyed one ruler.

British control arrived through separate agreements and military operations. Kalpi passed to the British in 1806, while Kalinjar fort was occupied in 1812. These were changes affecting particular places, not a single moment when all Bundelkhand was conquered. Banda became the headquarters of a southern Bundelkhand district in 1819, after this map interval.

A surviving 23-page handwritten account is titled Memoir on the Situation of Bundelcund in 1803. It includes royal family trees and annual revenue statements. Alexander Gerard presented it in 1828, but had not been in India in 1803. The archive therefore identifies it as a retrospective history, not his eyewitness diary.

Orchha’s Raja Mahal, Jahangir Mahal and Rani Mahal use square plans divided around open courtyards. Higher pavilions rise around these spaces. Gardens combined Mughal-style divisions, fort gardens and sacred groves with water management. Builders arranged views from above and open spaces below: the courtyards were as important to the design as the walls.

A small painted page now at LACMA shows Krishna and Radha meeting. Dated 1634, its image measures about 11 by 14 centimeters and uses opaque watercolor, gold and ink on paper. The museum cautiously attributes it to Orchha with a question mark. It illustrates poetry about relationships, rather than documenting an ordinary couple’s home.

Keshav Das’s Rasikapriya was composed in 1591 as a guide to poetry and feelings. A manuscript catalogued in 1899 preserves an eighteenth-century copy on European paper bearing a J. Whatman watermark. Books could carry ideas across generations, while even the paper records a connection beyond the local court.

A short language sample is the title “रसिकप्रिया” (Rasikapriyā), translated by the Smithsonian as “Connoisseur’s Delights.” The work dates to 1591 and belongs to Braj literary culture. The Devanagari spelling shown here is the modern transcription printed by IGNCA, not a claim to reproduce the handwriting of a surviving sixteenth-century page.

Traditional haveli farming could turn the same land into a shallow reservoir during the monsoon and a field afterward. Earthen banks held runoff; after the rains, water was released and crops grew in the moist soil. A 2022 research account traces this system back several centuries. A field could temporarily become a pond without ceasing to be a farm.

Keeping a haveli working required neighbors to repair banks and outlets and agree when water should be released. Water draining from one area could irrigate fields farther downhill. The study’s modern photographs show wheat on a drained reservoir bed. Food production depended on shared timing as well as individual effort.

Bundela reservoirs could include broad stairways down to the water and adjoining orchards. A 2014 national disaster-management study describes these elaborate tanks alongside simpler ponds and embankments. Waterworks served agriculture and displayed royal power, but they also needed continuing labor and money for maintenance.

IGNCA’s modern cultural account lists foods such as bara and fara and describes making little figures for festivals. It also records children’s games including marbles, gilli-danda and kabaddi. These are examples of remembered regional life, not a fixed menu or timetable for every child in 1800. Play did not require a palace full of toys.

A much later account reproduced in the 2014 drought study describes women fetching water while also cooking, farming and tending livestock. Girls sometimes cared for younger siblings while mothers searched for water, or spent hours fetching it themselves. Water shortages could therefore take time from both school and play. This describes modern conditions, not a measured household survey from 1800.

In Tikamgarh villages, research conducted from July 2011 to June 2012 recorded farmers’ and healers’ use of 41 plant species in livestock healthcare. The researcher interviewed knowledgeable elders, collected plants and preserved identified specimens. This documents care for animals and the transmission of practical knowledge; it neither establishes which remedies work nor proves that the same practices existed in 1800.

A modern Orchha homestay project reports two houses with composting toilets and another household, which keeps buffaloes, with a toilet linked to a biogas digester. The gas is used for cooking. Bathwater passes through a sand filter before irrigation. These are documented recent experiments in handling waste, not toilets reconstructed for the Bundela palaces.

The region’s political changes continued after 1815. In 1817 the Peshwa ceded his claims in British Bundelkhand; further annexations followed at different dates. Directly administered districts and princely states developed different relationships with colonial power. Bundelkhand’s communities and regional identity did not disappear when a treaty changed who collected revenue or claimed authority.

ending.text: The atlas’s 1815 endpoint is not a fall date. Maratha claims, individual princely states and British districts changed separately. Bundelkhand continued as a region, and Orchha remains a living town whose residents help maintain its monuments. Political sovereignty changed; communities, buildings and cultural practices carried on.
